title: Budget missing-object acquisition before searching a partial clone
applies_when: A local repository is a partial clone with a promisor remote, and source investigation needs only a few files or symbols at a pinned revision.
lesson: A read-looking Git command can fetch omitted objects. Before a broad revision-content search, list tree paths and choose the files that answer the current question. Read those pinned paths explicitly with a timeout and an acquisition budget. When a strictly local observation is required, supported Git versions offer --no-lazy-fetch or GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1. Treat a missing-object failure as incomplete source, never as proof that a symbol or implementation is absent. Explicitly acquire the needed objects before compilation or a complete source bundle; preserve the commit and blob identities.
avoid_when: A full build or repository-wide completeness claim may legitimately require all relevant objects. Do not impose local-only reads as a permanent execution gate, silently skip missing source, assume old Git versions support the switch, or infer lower token cost or higher PR yield from the documented mechanism alone.

evidence.note: Git documents demand-fetching missing objects from promisor remotes. Partial clone limits initial acquisition, not necessarily the cost of later content operations; it is independent of shallow history. This is mechanism evidence, not measured Scout efficiency.

This version documents --no-lazy-fetch and GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH, including using cat-file -e to inspect local object availability without demand-fetching. Verify availability for the actual installed Git.
